(b) Fixed or memorised routes are mentioned as part of the restrictive advice Kish rejects. His ability is
based on real-time interpretation of echoes, not merely route memory. Hence, option (b) is not the
correct answer.
(c) Kish’s method does not depend on sighted people giving him information. The passage stresses his
self-reliance and his ability to understand surroundings independently. Hence, option (c) is not the
correct answer.
(d) Kish is completely blind, and the passage does not suggest that he relies on visual images. His
recognition of objects comes through sound, not sight or visual memory. Hence, option (d) is not the
correct answer.
4.	Answer: D
Reference Line: “Kish is seeking — despite a lack of support from every mainstream blind
organization in America — nothing less than a profound reordering of the way the world views blind
people, and the way blind people view the world.”
Difficulty Level: Moderate
Explanation: (a) Lack of organisational support does not prove that Kish’s method is unsafe. The
passage gives several examples of successful navigation, so this option draws an unsupported
conclusion. Hence, option (a) is not the correct answer.
(b) Organisational support has no connection with the physical process of sound reflection. Echolocation
depends on clicks and echoes, not institutional approval. Hence, option (b) is not the correct answer.
(c) The passage does not say public curiosity ends because of institutional resistance. Some people even
admire Kish deeply, so this option misreads the social response. Hence, option (c) is not the correct
answer.
(d) The lack of support matters because Kish wants a broad change in how blindness is understood. If
major organisations resist him, his ideas may face difficulty in gaining wider acceptance. Hence, option
(d) is the correct answer.
5.	Answer: B
Reference Line: “He’s regarded by some in the blind community with deep veneration.”
Difficulty Level: Moderate
Explanation: (a) “Veneration” does not mean technical or professional approval. The line refers to
emotional respect from some people in the blind community, not formal validation of a method. Hence,
option (a) is not the correct answer.
(b) “Veneration” means deep respect, reverence, or admiration. In this context, it shows that some
members of the blind community hold Kish in very high regard. Hence, option (b) is the correct answer.
(c) Casual curiosity is too weak to capture the meaning of “veneration.” The word indicates serious
respect, not mere interest or fascination. Hence, option (c) is not the correct answer.
(d) Fearful avoidance is opposite to the sense of admiration conveyed by the sentence. The passage says
some people respect Kish, not that they avoid him out of fear. Hence, option (d) is not the correct
answer.
6.	Answer: C
Reference Line: “He’s tired of being told that the blind are best served by staying close to home,
sticking only to memorized routes, and depending on the unreliable benevolence of the sighted to do
anything beyond the most routine of tasks.”
Difficulty Level: Moderate

Explanation: (a) Mapping only fixed routes may seem useful, but it continues the same restricted
model Kish criticises. It keeps blind persons dependent on pre-set paths rather than developing
independent spatial confidence. Hence, option (a) is not the correct answer.
(b) Providing routine escorts may appear supportive, but it reinforces reliance on sighted assistance.
Kish objects to dependence on the “benevolence of the sighted,” especially beyond routine tasks. Hence,
option (b) is not the correct answer.
(c) Teaching self-navigation directly counters the restricted approach because it enables movement
beyond memorised routes and controlled spaces. This best reflects Kish’s emphasis on practical
independence. Hence, option (c) is the correct answer.
(d) Preventing outdoor exposure may reduce immediate risk, but it also deepens the confinement Kish
rejects. It treats safety as a reason to restrict autonomy. Hence, option (d) is not the correct answer.
7.	Answer: D
Reference Line: “Kish preaches complete and unfettered independence, even if the result produces the
occasional broken bone.”
Difficulty Level: Difficult
Explanation: (a) Caution is not rejected entirely in the passage, but Kish would not allow caution to
defeat autonomy altogether. The passage presents risk as manageable within independent living.
Hence, option (a) is not the correct answer.
(b) Supervision may be useful in limited training contexts, but the option wrongly makes supervision
the governing condition of skill. Kish’s philosophy moves beyond permanent dependence. Hence, option
(b) is not the correct answer.
(c) The possibility of injury does not prove that training is unwise. Kish’s own experience shows that
some risk may accompany meaningful independence without invalidating the method. Hence, option (c)
is not the correct answer.
(d) Kish would likely object that refusing outdoor training merely because of possible injury is
overprotective. It prevents blind students from developing the independence he values. Hence, option
(d) is the correct answer.
8.	Answer: B
Reference Line: “Kish is seeking — despite a lack of support from every mainstream blind
organization in America — nothing less than a profound reordering of the way the world views blind
people, and the way blind people view the world.”
Difficulty Level: Difficult
Explanation: (a) This option does not undermine the concern because the need for practice does not
show that Kish’s approach is unsafe or irrelevant. A skill may be difficult and still be worth teaching.
Hence, option (a) is not the correct answer.
(b) This option undermines the concern because it shows that Kish’s ability is not merely exceptional or
personal. If the skill can be taught through structured training, then his wider argument for changing
attitudes toward blindness becomes stronger. Hence, option (b) is the correct answer.
(c) This option only explains institutional hesitation. It does not reduce the concern about dependence
or prove that Kish’s method lacks practical value. Hence, option (c) is not the correct answer.
(d) This option is already accepted in the passage. Kish supports independence even when it carries
occasional risk, so this does not undermine the concerns raised. Hence, option (d) is not the correct
answer.

LAW PREP
— Tutorial—	MOCK AILET 10029 : ANSWER & EXPLANATIONS
9.	Answer: B
Reference Line: “For some time, the talks have been split over demands for the treaty to include plans
to reduce the amount of plastic that is being produced — a production cap.”
Difficulty Level: Moderate
Explanation: (a) This option misinterprets the word “cap” by linking it to the number of negotiators
rather than the subject of the treaty. The passage is concerned with plastic production, not attendance
at negotiations. Hence, option (a) is not the correct answer.
(b) The reference line clearly defines the production cap as a plan to reduce the amount of plastic being
produced. It directly captures the central dispute in the treaty talks. Hence, option (b) is the correct
answer.
(c) This option confuses production control with waste management or recycling. Recycling may deal
with plastic after use, but a production cap controls plastic at the stage of manufacture itself. Hence,
option (c) is not the correct answer.
(d) The passage mentions closed-door negotiations, but that has no connection with the meaning of
production cap. The cap relates to plastic output, not public speech or disclosure. Hence, option (d) is
not the correct answer.
10.	Answer: C
Reference Line: “A draft text for a final deal published on Friday included language for a global target
to reduce the amount of plastic made.”
Difficulty Level: Moderate
Explanation: (a) This option deals with procedure, not production. Delaying decisions may affect how
talks proceed, but it does not directly reduce the amount of plastic being manufactured. Hence, option
(a) is not the correct answer.
(b) Confidential negotiations may explain why details are not freely disclosed, but secrecy does not itself
address plastic output. It is a method of negotiation, not an environmental control. Hence, option (b) is
not the correct answer.
(c) This option directly reflects the proposal mentioned in the passage. A global target to reduce the
amount of plastic made is the treaty measure aimed at rising production. Hence, option (c) is the correct
answer.
(d) This option reflects the weaker approach preferred by countries opposing production cuts. Managing
waste may address pollution later, but it does not directly reduce plastic production. Hence, option (d) is
not the correct answer.
11.	Answer: D
Reference Line: “Plastic production is increasing, and could triple by 2050, projections show, piling
pressure on the environment and increasingly on human health.”
Difficulty Level: Moderate
Explanation: (a) This option wrongly shifts the focus from environmental harm to negotiators’
protection. The passage is concerned with the impact of rising plastic production on people and nature.
Hence, option (a) is not the correct answer.
(b) The passage does not suggest that production curbs remove government responsibility. On the
contrary, a treaty with production controls would require stronger collective responsibility from
countries. Hence, option (b) is not the correct answer.
(c) This option contradicts the passage’s concern about lobbyists influencing treaty ambition. The
passage treats such influence as a problem, not as a reason for supporting curbs. Hence, option (c) is not
the correct answer.

LAW PREP

(d) The reference line shows that rising production may intensify environmental and health risks.
Production curbs are supported because they target the source before pollution becomes harder to
control. Hence, option (d) is the correct answer.
12.	Answer: A
Reference Line: “Plastic microparticles and plastic chemicals have been detected in various human
biological systems, and research shows that global production controls are critical to bringing plastic
pollution under control.”
Difficulty Level: Moderate
Explanation: (a) This option correctly combines the key concerns in the passage: human health,
scientific evidence, and control of pollution. It captures why production controls are treated as essential,
not merely optional. Hence, option (a) is the correct answer.
(b) This option is contrary to the passage because the argument for production controls is supported by
research. The passage does not replace science with slogans; it relies on scientific concern. Hence,
option (b) is not the correct answer.
(c) This option reverses the logic of production controls. Such controls would increase treaty
responsibility by requiring action on plastic output, not help countries avoid obligations. Hence, option
(c) is not the correct answer.
(d) This option contradicts the purpose of production controls. The passage presents them as a way to
reduce plastic production, not as a method to permit expansion with less scrutiny. Hence, option (d) is
not the correct answer.
13.	Answer: D
Reference Line: “The ambitious wording reflects the growing momentum from 102 nations that have
banded together over the last few months and days to demand that plastic curbs are included.”
Difficulty Level: Moderate
Explanation: (a) This option is identified as a practical challenge because the passage states that
consensus-based decision-making has proved impossible. Therefore, it is a real procedural obstacle in
the negotiations. Hence, option (a) is not the correct answer.
(b) This option is also identified in the passage as a difficulty because unresolved voting rules prevented
majority voting from moving the talks forward. It is a procedural challenge, not an absent factor.
Hence, option (b) is not the correct answer.
(c) This option is identified as a challenge because some countries oppose the inclusion of production
cuts in the treaty text. This resistance is central to the deadlock described in the passage. Hence, option
(c) is not the correct answer.
(d) This option is not identified as a challenge because the passage says the opposite: 102 nations have
joined together to demand plastic curbs. Therefore, absence of support is not a difficulty here. Hence,
option (d) is the correct answer.
14.	Answer: A
Reference Line: “But some warned that fragile progress could disappear again in the last stages of
negotiations over the weekend.”
Difficulty Level: Moderate
Explanation: (a) This option correctly captures the contextual meaning of the phrase. The passage
suggests that some progress had been made after a long deadlock, but that progress was still weak and
could collapse during the final stage. Hence, option (a) is the correct answer.

LAW PREP

(b) This option wrongly shifts the phrase from negotiation to science. The passage does not say that
research findings were being removed. Hence, option (b) is not the correct answer.
(c) This option overstates the situation because the treaty had not become final or legally binding. The
phrase shows uncertainty, not final settlement. Hence, option (c) is not the correct answer.
(d) This option misreads the passage. The phrase does not mean that waste systems would replace
negotiations; it means diplomatic progress may fail. Hence, option (d) is not the correct answer.
15.	Answer: C
Reference Line: “Their collective voice on production signals an important shift.”
Difficulty Level: Difficult
Explanation: (a) This option contradicts the passage because the coalition supports plastic curbs, not
waste management alone. The author’s point is that production must be addressed directly. Hence,
option (a) is not the correct answer.
(b) This option is inconsistent with the passage’s criticism of older industrial interests. The author
implies that the treaty should serve people and future generations, not industries of the past. Hence,
option (b) is not the correct answer.
(c) This option captures the assumption behind the discussion of the coalition. The author treats the
collective pressure of 102 nations as capable of changing the treaty’s direction and ambition. Hence,
option (c) is the correct answer.
(d) This option goes against the passage’s use of health-related evidence. The author links plastic
pollution to human biological systems, so health evidence is central, not irrelevant. Hence, option (d) is
not the correct answer.
16.	Answer: B
Reference Line: “It’s about minimising human suffering.”
Difficulty Level: Moderate
Explanation: (a) This option mistakes a procedural feature for the treaty’s moral purpose. Secrecy
may describe how negotiations happen, but it is not the deeper motivation for production curbs. Hence,
option (a) is not the correct answer.
(b) This option directly reflects the quoted line. The author frames the treaty as a human-centred effort
aimed at reducing suffering caused by plastic pollution and its wider effects. Hence, option (b) is the
correct answer.
(c) This option contradicts the passage’s tone toward older industries. The passage suggests that the
treaty should not be shaped by industries of the previous century. Hence, option (c) is not the correct
answer.
(d) This option wrongly elevates procedure above purpose. Voting rules matter to negotiations, but the
deeper motivation described in the passage is human welfare, not procedural dominance. Hence, option
(d) is not the correct answer.
17.	Answer: B
Reference Line: “But many public statements and documents shared by Russia, Iran, Saudi Arabia
and some others show that these countries oppose production cuts and want the treaty to tackle
pollution by managing waste.”
Difficulty Level: Moderate
Explanation: (a) This option is misleading because “output restraint” would mean limiting plastic
production, which the passage says these countries oppose. It reverses their stated position. Hence,
option (a) is not the correct answer.

LAW PREP
— Tutorial—	MOCK AILET 10029 : ANSWER & EXPLANATIONS
(b) The passage clearly shows that these countries prefer addressing pollution through waste
management rather than production cuts. This captures their lower-ambition approach. Hence, option
(b) is the correct answer.
(c) Island states are described as part of the ambitious bloc demanding plastic curbs. This option
confuses the Low Ambition Coalition with the countries pushing for stronger production controls.
Hence, option (c) is not the correct answer.
(d) Voting reform relates to procedural gridlock, but the passage does not identify it as the Low
Ambition Coalition’s position. Their relevant stance concerns production cuts and waste management.
Hence, option (d) is not the correct answer.
18.	Answer: A
Reference Line: “The gridlock might have been resolved by a vote to move things forward with a
majority decision, but that has been stymied by earlier disagreements over the voting rules, which have
not been resolved.”
Difficulty Level: Moderate
Explanation: (a) This option correctly captures the passage’s procedural point. Majority voting could
have helped break the deadlock, but unresolved disagreements over voting rules prevented that
possibility. Hence, option (a) is the correct answer.
(b) This option overstates the effect of majority voting. The passage says voting might have moved
things forward, not that it would automatically guarantee production caps. Hence, option (b) is not the
correct answer.
(c) This option contradicts the passage because consensus has proved difficult and voting rules remain
unresolved. There was no unanimous agreement allowing voting to replace consensus. Hence, option (c)
is not the correct answer.
(d) This option introduces an unsupported claim. The passage raises concern about lobbyists’ influence,
but it does not say they were empowered to vote for national delegations. Hence, option (d) is not the
correct answer.
19.	Answer: C
Reference Line: “He argues that democracy depends not only on elections, but also on informed
participation and open discussion.”
Difficulty Level: Moderate
Explanation: (a) This option is incomplete because Keller does not treat elections alone as sufficient. It
also wrongly limits disagreement, while the passage values open discussion. Hence, option (a) is not the
correct answer.
(b) This option misrepresents Keller’s view. He does not argue that institutions should be protected
from public pressure; he values civic engagement and accountability. Hence, option (b) is not the correct
answer.
(c) This option accurately reflects Keller’s argument. He believes democracy requires informed citizens
and open public discussion in addition to elections. Hence, option (c) is the correct answer.
(d) This option contradicts the passage because controlled debate would weaken democratic life. Keller
supports open discussion, not leadership-controlled debate. Hence, option (d) is not the correct answer.
20.	Answer: C
Reference Line: “She studies issues such as inequality, labour rights, gender justice, and access to
education, showing how these concerns become part of larger political struggles.”
Difficulty Level: Difficult

LAW PREP
— Tutorial—	MOCK AILET 10029 : ANSWER & EXPLANATIONS
Explanation: (a) This option misrepresents Collins’s argument because she presents social concerns as
becoming part of larger political struggles. Avoiding collective struggle would weaken, rather than
support, the process of reform described in the passage. Hence, option (a) is not the correct answer.
(b) Collins does not portray governments as acting in isolation from society. The passage suggests that
public demands and reform movements influence how governments and institutions respond. Hence,
option (b) is not the correct answer.
(c) This option correctly captures the inference that social issues become politically significant when
people organise around them. Collins links inequality, labour rights, gender justice, and education to
wider struggles for reform. Hence, option (c) is the correct answer.
(d) Collins specifically rejects the idea that reform comes from isolated leadership alone. Detachment
from activism would contradict her emphasis on collective pressure and public mobilisation. Hence,
option (d) is not the correct answer.
21.	Answer: A
Reference Line: “Keller explains how misinformation, political polarization, and unequal access to
power can weaken democratic systems.”
Difficulty Level: Moderate
Explanation: (a) This option correctly explains the phrase in context. It suggests that some groups
have greater ability than others to influence political decisions, institutions, or outcomes. Hence, option
(a) is the correct answer.
(b) This option gives the opposite meaning. Equal opportunity would strengthen democracy, while
Keller is describing a weakening condition. Hence, option (b) is not the correct answer.
(c) This option is incorrect because neutral distribution implies fairness. The phrase points to
imbalance, not neutrality. Hence, option (c) is not the correct answer.
(d) This option exaggerates the phrase. Keller does not say public discussion disappears completely; he
says democracy is weakened by unequal access to power. Hence, option (d) is not the correct answer.
22.	Answer: A
Reference Line: “He explains that national identity is influenced not only by history and language,
but also by social memory, public institutions, and political narratives.”
Difficulty Level: Moderate
Explanation: (a) Both statements are directly supported by the passage, and the reason explains the
assertion. Hale’s view expands national identity beyond history and language by adding social and
political influences. Hence, option (a) is the correct answer.
(b) Although both statements are true, this option fails because the reason is not merely related to the
assertion. It provides the exact basis for saying that Hale’s view goes beyond history and language.
Hence, option (b) is not the correct answer.
(c) The assertion is true, but the reason is not false. The passage expressly mentions social memory,
institutions, and narratives as additional influences on national identity. Hence, option (c) is not the
correct answer.
(d) The assertion is not false because Hale clearly rejects a narrow understanding of identity based only
on history and language. The reason is true, but it cannot stand against a false assertion here. Hence,
option (d) is not the correct answer.

LAW PREP
— Tutorial—	MOCK AILET 10029 : ANSWER & EXPLANATIONS
23.	Answer: C
Reference Line: “Keller examines the relationship between citizens, political institutions, and public
debate”; “Collins explains how governments, activists, and institutions respond to demands for reform”;
“Hale examines how societies balance unity with individual freedom.”
Difficulty Level: Difficult
Explanation: (a) Institutional political order is a plausible distractor because Keller and Collins both
discuss institutions, and Hale also refers to public institutions. However, this option is too narrow
because it does not fully include public debate, collective reform, citizenship, identity, and social
belonging. Hence, option (a) is not the correct answer.
(b) Collective reform action fits Collins strongly because she directly links social progress with collective
action and public pressure. However, it does not equally capture Keller’s focus on democratic
participation or Hale’s focus on national identity and civic belonging. Hence, option (b) is not the correct
answer.
(c) Civic-political life is the broad concern connecting all three books. Keller discusses citizens and
democratic debate, Collins discusses reform through public pressure, and Hale discusses identity,
citizenship, and social trust within political communities. Hence, option (c) is the correct answer.
(d) National-cultural belonging fits Hale most closely because his book studies nationality, culture, and
belonging. However, it does not sufficiently cover Keller’s emphasis on democratic debate or Collins’s
emphasis on social movements and reform. Hence, option (d) is not the correct answer.
24,	Answer: C
Reference Line: “At the same time, he shows how civic engagement and public accountability
strengthen political life.”
Difficulty Level: Difficult
Explanation: (a) Keller supports civic engagement, but he does not suggest that collective action
should replace institutions altogether. His framework depends on citizens, institutions, debate, and
accountability working together. Hence, option (a) is not the correct answer.
(b) This option creates an artificial limitation that is not found in Keller’s view. He discusses civic
engagement broadly, including protests and public debate, not only situations where elections are
absent. Hence, option (b) is not the correct answer.
(c) This option properly applies Keller’s reasoning to Collins’s focus on political movements. Keller
would likely value collective mobilisation but insist that it strengthens democracy only when linked
with public accountability. Hence, option (c) is the correct answer.
(d) Keller would not support ignoring media and debate because both are part of his analysis of
democratic life. The passage specifically mentions media and public discussion as relevant to
democratic functioning. Hence, option (d) is not the correct answer.
25.	Answer: D
Reference Line: “He argues that strong societies require both shared civic values and respect for
difference.”
Difficulty Level: Moderate
Explanation: (a) This option is incorrect because Hale does not support sameness. He argues for
shared civic values along with respect for difference. Hence, option (a) is not the correct answer.
(b) This option is too narrow. Social memory is one influence on national identity, but Hale also refers to
institutions, narratives, civic values, and diversity. Hence, option (b) is not the correct answer.
(c) This option misrepresents Hale’s view. He discusses balancing unity with individual freedom, not
treating freedom as a threat to trust. Hence, option (c) is not the correct answer.

LAW PREP
— Tutorial—	MOCK AILET 10029 : ANSWER & EXPLANATIONS
(d) This option correctly combines both parts of Hale’s view. A strong society needs common civic values
as well as respect for pluralism and difference. Hence, option (d) is the correct answer.
26.	Answer: B
Reference Line: “Through historical and contemporary examples, Collins explains how governments,
activists, and institutions respond to demands for reform.”
Difficulty Level: Moderate
Explanation: (a) Keller discusses democratic debate and institutions, but he is not the thinker most
directly linked with reform demands in the passage. Hence, option (a) is not the correct answer.
(b) Collins is directly connected with reform movements, public pressure, and institutional response.
The reference line clearly supports this answer. Hence, option (b) is the correct answer.
(c) Hale focuses on nationality, identity, belonging, and social trust. His concern is not primarily
institutional response to reform movements. Hence, option (c) is not the correct answer.
(d) This option overgeneralises the three authors. Cultural diversity is especially connected with Hale,
not equally with all three. Hence, option (d) is not the correct answer.
27.	Answer: C
Reference Line: “Referring to debates on migration, globalization, and cultural diversity, Hale
examines how societies balance unity with individual freedom.”
Difficulty Level: Moderate
Explanation: (a) Electoral legitimacy may fit Keller’s discussion of democracy more closely, but Hale’s
focus is nationality, culture, identity, and belonging. Hence, option (a) is not the correct answer.
(b) Labour mobilisation is more closely connected with Collins’s focus on labour rights and social
movements. It is not the issue Hale most directly examines. Hence, option (b) is not the correct answer.
(c) Migration and globalisation debates directly raise questions of nationality, culture, diversity, and
belonging. This option best fits Hale’s thematic focus. Hence, option (c) is the correct answer.
(d) Media accountability is closer to Keller’s concerns about public debate and misinformation. Hale’s
discussion is centred on identity, citizenship, and cultural diversity. Hence, option (d) is not the correct
answer.
28.	Answer: A
Reference Line: “Getting along and getting ahead requires coordinating with others, either in
cooperation as friends, spouses, teammates, and coworkers, or in competition as adversaries, opponents,
or rivals.”
Difficulty Level: Moderate
Explanation: (a) This option is correct because the passage itself immediately clarifies the meaning of
“adversaries” through the accompanying words “opponents” and “rivals.” The surrounding contrast
between cooperation and competition makes it clear that the term refers to people who stand against us
in struggle, contest, or conflict. Hence, option (a) is the correct answer.
(b) This option is not correct because “distant strangers” merely suggests unfamiliarity or lack of
personal closeness. The passage is not describing people who are unknown to us, but those who actively
occupy the competitive side of social interaction. Hence, option (b) is not the correct answer.
(c) This option is not correct because “silent observers” would refer to passive onlookers who do not
participate in the action. The passage clearly places adversaries within active competition, which
requires direct engagement rather than detached observation. Hence, option (c) is not the correct
answer.

LAW PREP
— Tutorial—	MOCK AILET 10029 : ANSWER & EXPLANATIONS
(d) This option is not correct because “trusted partners” belongs to the cooperative side of the sentence,
not the competitive one. The author deliberately contrasts friends and coworkers with adversaries, so
this choice reverses the intended meaning. Hence, option (d) is not the correct answer.
29.	Answer: C
Reference Line: “Our daily lives are guided by inferences about what others think, believe, feel, and
want. This is your sixth sense at work.”
Difficulty Level: Moderate
Explanation: (a) This option is not correct because the passage does not describe the “sixth sense” as
supernatural foresight or future prediction. The author is discussing an ordinary human social faculty
that helps us interpret other people’s mental states in daily interaction. Hence, option (a) is not the
correct answer.
(b) This option is not correct because careful speech concerns how we express ourselves, whereas the
passage focuses on how we understand others. The “sixth sense” here is about perception and inference,
not about speaking cautiously or politely. Hence, option (b) is not the correct answer.
(c) This option is correct because the author directly defines the phrase through our constant attempts
to infer what others think, believe, feel, and want. The expression is therefore a metaphor for social
mind-reading rather than for any mystical or physical capacity. Hence, option (c) is the correct answer.
(d) This option is not correct because bodily balance is a physical sense connected with movement and
coordination. The passage instead deals with psychological and social interpretation, showing that the
phrase refers to understanding minds, not managing the body. Hence, option (d) is not the correct
answer.
30.	Answer: C
Reference Line: “No human being succeeds in life alone.” / “Getting along and getting ahead requires
coordinating with others, either in cooperation as friends, spouses, teammates, and coworkers, or in
competition as adversaries, opponents, or rivals.”
Difficulty Level: Difficult
Explanation: (a) This option is incorrect because Statement 1 is not true. The passage clearly says
that no human being succeeds in life alone, so the idea that people can succeed entirely without
depending on others contradicts the passage. Hence, option (a) is not the correct answer.
(b) This option is incorrect because both statements are not true. Statement 2 is supported by the
passage, but Statement 1 is false because the author stresses the social nature of human success.
Hence, option (b) is not the correct answer.
(c) This option is correct because Statement 1 contradicts the passage, while Statement 2 is directly
supported by it. The author argues that humans must coordinate with others in both cooperation and
competition. Hence, option (c) is the correct answer.
(d) This option is incorrect because it reverses the truth of the statements. Statement 1 is false, while
Statement 2 is true according to the passage. Hence, option (d) is not the correct answer.
31.	Answer: D
Reference Line: “One of the biggest barriers to understanding others is excessive egocentrism.”
Difficulty Level: Moderate
Explanation: (a) This option is not correct because fear of social judgment refers to anxiety about what
other people think of us. The passage is instead concerned with the difficulty of moving beyond one’s
own point of view while attempting to understand someone else. Hence, option (a) is not the correct
answer.

LAW PREP
— Tutorial—	MOCK AILET 10029 : ANSWER & EXPLANATIONS
(b) This option is not correct because dependence on group approval suggests conformity and a need for
acceptance. The passage defines egocentrism differently: as being so centered in one’s own experiences
and beliefs that one cannot fully appreciate other perspectives. Hence, option (b) is not the correct
answer.
(c) This option is not correct because the passage does not define egocentrism as loss or rejection of
memory. Although memory bias appears later in the household experiment, the core concept here is
